reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in Educational services (NAICS 61) at 30.0% of firms, measured as the share answering yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks. The same series shows a prior period figure of 35.5%, and the survey first asked the question in September 2023. The Census Bureau notes that an S in this series means the value is suppressed, so not every cut of the data is published.

The clearest picture of what education organizations actually run comes from the federal guidance page, where the Department of Education publishes an inventory of its own AI use cases. Those include CAISY, described as delivering real-time insights, predictive analytics and intelligent automation to streamline repetitive tasks; Grammarly's AI assistant for written communication; Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration in meetings, interviews and lectures; and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. The Department of Education also lists narrower tasks: generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in multiple programming languages, returning R code for data analysis, converting data types such as a county name into its FIPS code, generating mock datasets for testing, training employees on prompt engineering, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, extracting action items from public articles and policies, testing filters and data loss prevention against fabricated prohibited prompts, and drafting position descriptions and public messages.

The regulatory posture in this material is set by the Department of Education, which frames its guidance around permissible use, risk and procurement for US education, and describes its OCIO as supporting adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement and responsible and secure usage, in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. That is the posture a school or system is operating inside, and it is stated as a matter of compliance and risk management rather than as a mandate to adopt.

On where money and vendors concentrate, HolonIQ is the market intelligence source in this set, describing itself as a platform for impact market intelligence that sizes addressable markets, quantifies demand, forecasts scenarios at varying rates of growth, and scores impact with rubrics and ratings to power policy, procurement and investment decisions. HolonIQ says it serves governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms and investors, and that global media rely on it for insight and data on the global impact economy. The site's own description of HolonIQ adds that it covers EdTech funding, digital transformation and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed and workforce learning.

The education sections catalogued here track the courses and credentials the field uses, and the catalog page reports 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, each with one verified source and re-verified daily. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The page draws a distinction between university courses structured around exam-driven theory and industry courses described as code-first or hands-on, and it states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken. Costs and renewal cycles are tracked by pointing at issuer pages.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow set of conclusions. The Census Bureau gives a measured adoption rate for the sector and shows it moving between periods. The Department of Education shows the shape of legitimate use in an education setting, mostly drafting, summarizing, transcription, code assistance and internal analysis, alongside an explicit compliance frame. HolonIQ shows that a market intelligence layer exists for sizing and forecasting. None of these sources reports ROI figures, cost savings or outcome gains for education deployments, and the course catalog explicitly declines to report enrollment or completion, so the evidence here describes activity and posture rather than proven returns.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
